ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Volume-based joint contrastive alignment versus pairwise InfoNCE on a shared public set
PROPOSAL: Six clients hold different architectures (ResNet-18, ViT-Small, ConvNeXt-Tiny, two small BERT variants reading captions, and a wav2vec-style audio encoder) and different local tasks. Each client projects public-set representations into 128 dimensions; the server computes a volume-based joint contrastive loss over the six embeddings of each public instance and returns target embeddings. Public data: 50000 unlabeled image-caption pairs from COCO. We read local accuracy on CIFAR-100, Flowers-102 and a small audio-event client after 30 communication rounds, averaged over 3 seeds.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; pairwise InfoNCE summed over client pairs; alignment to a single anchor client; a centered kernel alignment proximal term; a public set with shuffled instance correspondence to test that gains come from matched instances.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: The joint loss should beat pairwise InfoNCE by 1 to 3 accuracy points, with the gap growing as clients are added. It may fail if the volume term becomes ill-conditioned for low-rank embeddings, in which case a regularized form is needed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Determinant-style joint contrastive alignment of large encoders across temperature and width sweeps
PROPOSAL: Twelve clients hold large architectures (ViT-Large, ConvNeXt-Base, ResNet-152, Swin-B, BERT-large variants on captions, and audio transformers) with different local tasks. Representations of public instances are projected into 512 dimensions and the server evaluates one volume-based joint contrastive loss over the twelve embeddings per instance. Public data: 118000 image-caption pairs from COCO. Local accuracy on CIFAR-100, Flowers-102 and an audio-event client is read after 100 rounds, over 10 seeds, a sweep of 5 temperatures and 4 projection widths, restarting from newly pretrained encoders whenever a setting changes.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; pairwise InfoNCE summed over client pairs; alignment to a single anchor client; a centered kernel alignment proximal term; a public set with shuffled instance correspondence at the largest scale.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: The joint loss should outperform pairwise InfoNCE at all temperatures, with a gain of 1 to 3 points that persists across projection widths. It may fail if the volume term saturates once embeddings are high-dimensional and nearly orthogonal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantized low-dimensional embedding exchange for communication-efficient heterogeneous collaboration
PROPOSAL: Eight clients with different backbones (MobileNetV3, ResNet-34, DeiT-Tiny, DistilBERT) send only public-set embeddings, projected to a small width and quantized to eight bits, and receive aligned targets from the server. Public set: 20000 unlabeled STL-10 images with generated captions. We measure local task accuracy against bytes transmitted per round over twenty rounds with three seeds, comparing projection widths 16, 64 and 256.
CONTROLS: Uncompressed float32 exchange; random projection without learned alignment; magnitude-based sparsification of embeddings; parameter-sharing FedAvg on the homogeneous subset as an upper reference; local-only training.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Eight-bit 64-dimensional exchange should stay within one point of uncompressed accuracy at roughly sixteen times less traffic. It fails if quantization noise erases the fine joint structure needed by the audio task clients.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned product-quantization codebooks for embedding exchange in a large client population
PROPOSAL: Sixty-four clients with varied backbones (EfficientNet-B4, ViT-Base, Swin-S, RoBERTa-base) send projected public-set embeddings compressed by a product-quantization codebook that is relearned at each round, and receive aligned targets. Public set: 100000 unlabeled ImageNet images with generated captions. We record accuracy and traffic over 60 rounds with 8 seeds, on a grid of 6 codebook sizes and 5 projection widths, re-pretraining all backbones when a setting changes.
CONTROLS: Uncompressed float32 exchange; random projection without learned alignment; magnitude-based sparsification of embeddings; parameter-sharing FedAvg on a homogeneous subset; local-only training for the whole population.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Codebook exchange should retain accuracy within one point of uncompressed exchange with much lower traffic, at most settings of the grid. It fails if the relearned codebook drifts between rounds and destabilizes alignment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Finite-sample bound for joint multi-view contrastive alignment, checked on Gaussian synthetic views
PROPOSAL: We derive a lower bound on the total correlation among the representations of M models that the volume-based joint contrastive loss maximizes, with an explicit finite-sample term in the number of public instances and a dependence on the number of models. We then check the bound on synthetic Gaussian views with known total correlation, using M equal to 3, 5 and 8 linear encoders trained by gradient descent, 5 seeds, and public set sizes from 1000 to 20000.
CONTROLS: The bound for pairwise InfoNCE summed over pairs; the exact analytic total correlation of the Gaussian generator; a loose bound without the finite-sample term; a permuted-view sample to confirm the estimator is near zero without dependence.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: The joint bound should track the true total correlation closely while the pairwise sum saturates early as M grows. It could fail by being loose at small public set sizes, where the finite-sample term dominates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tightness study of a joint contrastive bound on deep-network views over many public set sizes
PROPOSAL: We derive a lower bound on the total correlation among the representations of M models that the volume-based joint contrastive loss maximizes, with a finite-sample term. Validation uses synthetic views passed through random deep nonlinear generators with known dependence; M takes values three, five, eight, twelve and sixteen, nonlinear six-layer encoders are trained, 20 seeds are drawn, and public set sizes range over 1000, 5000, 20000, 50000 and 100000 with encoders retrained at each size.
CONTROLS: The bound for pairwise InfoNCE summed over pairs; the analytic total correlation of the generator; a loose bound without the finite-sample term; a permuted-view sample for the estimator at every size.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: The joint bound should follow the true dependence with a gap shrinking as public set size grows, while the pairwise sum saturates. It could fail by being loose for the largest M, where estimation variance across seeds dominates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effect of public dataset size and domain on knowledge transfer across tasks of different logit sizes
PROPOSAL: Ten clients solve different tasks (CIFAR-10 classification, Oxford Pets, SVHN digits, depth regression on NYU subsets, and a text sentiment task) with different architectures. Alignment runs through a joint contrastive loss on a public set, which we vary: 5000, 20000 or 50000 unlabeled images drawn from either in-domain COCO, out-of-domain textures, or a blend. Each condition is run for 25 rounds with 3 seeds, and per-client gain over local-only is reported.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; alignment on a public set of random noise images; pairwise InfoNCE on the same public sets; a logit-distillation baseline restricted to clients sharing label sets.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Gains should rise with public set size and be larger in-domain, with a plateau near 20000 images. It may fail if out-of-domain textures turn out to be about as useful, which would suggest that data diversity matters more than domain match.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling public pools and domains for cross-task knowledge transfer among many architectures
PROPOSAL: Forty clients solve different tasks (ImageNet-100 classification, Food-101, SVHN, depth regression on full NYU, segmentation on VOC, and several text tasks) with varied architectures. Alignment uses a joint contrastive loss on a public pool whose size is 5000, 20000, 50000, 100000 or 200000 images from in-domain COCO, out-of-domain textures, satellite scenes, or blends of these. Each of the conditions is run for eighty rounds with six seeds, retraining all clients from pretrained weights.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; alignment on a public pool of random noise images; pairwise InfoNCE on identical pools; a logit-distillation baseline restricted to clients with matching label sets.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Gains should grow with pool size up to a plateau and be larger in-domain. It may fail if the plateau arrives early, so that the largest pools bring no change over the moderate ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Membership-inference audit of embedding-only collaboration among fine-tuned foundation models
PROPOSAL: Five clients each fine-tune a different pre-trained foundation model (CLIP ViT-B/16, DINOv2-Small, a 125M-parameter language model, a speech encoder, and a ResNet-50) with LoRA on a small private dataset, and share only public-set embeddings. We mount a shadow-model membership-inference attack against the server-visible embeddings and compare its AUC with a parameter-sharing baseline, over 15 rounds and 3 seeds, while recording task accuracy.
CONTROLS: Parameter-sharing federated LoRA on the shared-architecture subset; local-only fine-tuning; embeddings from the frozen foundation models without fine-tuning; a random-guess attack to calibrate the AUC.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Attack AUC on embedding-only exchange should stay near 0.5 to 0.55 while parameter sharing leaks more, with accuracy within a point of the sharing baseline. It may fail if embeddings of memorized private samples remain separable.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-scale privacy and utility sweep for embedding-only collaboration among fine-tuned foundation models
PROPOSAL: Sixteen clients fine-tune different pre-trained foundation models (CLIP ViT-L/14, DINOv2-Giant, 7B-parameter language models, Whisper-Large, and ResNet-101) with LoRA at 4 ranks on private datasets, and share only public-set embeddings. A shadow-model membership-inference attack is mounted over 60 rounds and 10 seeds with 5 shadow-model counts, retraining every shadow model whenever the rank changes, and task accuracy is logged.
CONTROLS: Parameter-sharing federated LoRA on the shared-architecture subset; local-only fine-tuning; embeddings from frozen foundation models; a random-guess attack to calibrate the AUC at each rank.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Attack AUC on embedding-only exchange should stay between 0.5 and 0.55 for every rank, while parameter sharing leaks more. It may fail at high ranks, where fine-tuned encoders memorize more of their private samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extending joint alignment to three modalities: image, text and audio clients
PROPOSAL: Nine clients cover three modalities (image: ResNet-50, ViT-Small, EfficientNet-B0; text: DistilBERT, MiniLM, a small GPT-2; audio: wav2vec-small, AST, a CNN spectrogram model). Public data are 30000 triplets of image, caption and audio narration from Flickr8k-style corpora. The server applies a volume-based joint contrastive loss across the three modalities; we measure retrieval recall at ten and local task accuracy over thirty rounds and three seeds.
CONTROLS: Heuristic contrastive regularization between two modalities applied to all modality pairs; pairwise InfoNCE averaged over pairs; local-only training; a variant dropping the audio client to test dependence on the third modality.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Joint alignment should improve three-way retrieval recall by several points over pairwise averaging and help the audio clients most. It may fail if the audio narration is too weakly correlated with captions to add shared structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint alignment of five modalities with large clients and repeated cross-modal retrieval evaluation
PROPOSAL: Thirty clients span five modalities (image: ViT-Large, ConvNeXt-Base; text: BERT-large, RoBERTa-large; audio: AST, Whisper encoder; video: VideoMAE; depth: DPT), each using large models. Public data are 400000 aligned tuples drawn from large web corpora. A volume-based joint contrastive loss acts across the five modalities; retrieval recall at 10 and task accuracy are measured over 100 rounds and 10 seeds, with 5 retrieval protocols and every modality subset evaluated separately.
CONTROLS: Heuristic contrastive regularization between two modalities applied to all modality pairs; pairwise InfoNCE averaged over pairs; local-only training; variants removing one modality at a time.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Joint alignment should lift multi-way retrieval recall over pairwise averaging, with gains growing as modalities are added. It may fail if weakly correlated modalities such as depth add noise to the shared space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling the number of clients: does joint alignment capture dependencies that pairwise losses miss?
PROPOSAL: We vary the number of clients among 3, 6, 12 and 24, each with a randomly assigned architecture from a pool of eight (ResNet, MobileNet, ViT, ConvNeXt, DistilBERT and others) and a distinct local task. The public set has 30000 unlabeled images. Joint volume-based and pairwise InfoNCE alignment are compared on local accuracy and on a probe of how well a held-out client can be predicted from the others, across 25 rounds and 3 seeds.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; pairwise InfoNCE summed over client pairs; a joint loss computed on random client subsets of size three; a centered kernel alignment proximal term as a model-agnostic baseline.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The advantage of joint alignment should widen as clients are added, since pairwise losses ignore higher-order structure. It could fail if a plateau appears beyond 12 clients, or if subset-based joint losses recover most of the gain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Client count sweep with architecture pool resampling for joint versus pairwise alignment
PROPOSAL: We vary the number of clients among 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96 and 128, each with architecture drawn from a pool of twenty large models and a distinct local task, resampling the assignment ten times per count. The public set holds 200000 unlabeled images. Joint volume-based and pairwise InfoNCE alignment are compared on local accuracy and on a held-out client prediction probe, across eighty rounds and five seeds per assignment.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; pairwise InfoNCE summed over client pairs; a joint loss computed on random client subsets of size three; a centered kernel alignment proximal term as a baseline for the whole range.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The advantage of joint alignment should widen with client count since pairwise losses miss higher-order structure. It could fail if the gain stops growing beyond 24 clients, or if subset-based joint losses recover most of it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Server aggregation of representations: anchor-based, Gramian-based and kernel-alignment variants compared
PROPOSAL: 7 clients with distinct architectures and tasks (CIFAR-100, Pets, text topic classification, tabular regression, and others) exchange public-set embeddings. The server aggregates them three ways: an anchor-based average of embeddings, a Gramian-based joint loss, and a model-agnostic proximal term from centered kernel alignment. We compare local accuracy and round-to-round stability over 25 rounds, with 3 seeds, on a public set of 25000 samples.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; no aggregation with embeddings shared once and never updated; a shuffled public set; knowledge distillation among the clients sharing logit sizes; sensitivity of kernel alignment to the representation layer chosen.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: The Gramian-based joint loss should give the best local accuracy and steadier training than anchors, with kernel alignment between them. It may fail if the Gramian form is unstable without regularization on poorly conditioned embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-client comparison of anchor, Gramian and kernel-alignment aggregation under many hyperparameters
PROPOSAL: Forty clients with distinct architectures and tasks (ImageNet-100, Food-101, text topics, tabular regression, speech commands, and others) send public-set embeddings. The server aggregates by anchor averaging, a Gramian-based joint loss, or a centered kernel alignment term, each tuned on six learning rates, four temperatures and three layers. Local accuracy and stability are measured over 80 rounds with 8 seeds on a public set of 200000 samples, retraining clients for every cell.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; no aggregation with embeddings shared once and never updated; a shuffled public set; knowledge distillation among clients with equal logit sizes; sensitivity of kernel alignment to layer choice at each scale.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: The Gramian-based loss should yield the best local accuracy and steadier training than anchors, with kernel alignment between them. It may fail if gains vanish once each method is tuned to its best settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mixed task families: negative transfer among classification, regression and segmentation clients
PROPOSAL: Nine clients with different architectures solve three kinds of task: classification (CIFAR-100, Pets), regression (age estimation on UTKFace, depth on NYU) and dense prediction (VOC segmentation with a small U-Net, and a DeepLab model). Alignment uses a joint contrastive loss over 20000 public images. We report per-client change from local-only and test whether clients of one family lose accuracy when aligned with another, over 25 rounds and 3 seeds.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; alignment restricted within each task family; pairwise InfoNCE across all clients; a variant weighting alignment by task similarity estimated from the embeddings.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: Most clients should gain, with dense prediction clients gaining least and a few regression clients losing slightly under cross-family alignment. It may fail if the shared space is dominated by classification clients, harming the others.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-family alignment among many task types with repeated retraining and weighting sweeps
PROPOSAL: Thirty-six clients solve five kinds of task: classification (ImageNet-100, Food-101), regression (age on UTKFace, depth on NYU), segmentation (VOC with DeepLab and Mask2Former), keypoints (COCO pose), and detection. Alignment uses a joint contrastive loss over 150000 public images. We report per-client change from local-only and test negative transfer across families, over eighty rounds with eight seeds and six alignment strengths, retraining all clients at every strength.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; alignment restricted within each task family; pairwise InfoNCE across all clients; a variant weighting alignment by task similarity estimated from embeddings at each alignment strength.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: Most clients should gain, with dense prediction clients gaining least and some regression clients losing slightly across families. It may fail if the shared space is dominated by classification clients as strength rises.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Public data selection for heterogeneous collaboration: curated, random and synthetic pools
PROPOSAL: Eight clients with mixed architectures and tasks align on public pools of 20000 samples built in three ways: random COCO images, images chosen by embedding diversity (greedy farthest-point), and diffusion-generated images from class-agnostic prompts. A joint contrastive loss is used for 25 rounds with 3 seeds. We compare local accuracy per pool and under a shift where local data come from a different domain than the pool.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; a pool of pure noise images; a pool of the same size drawn from the clients' own training data (an upper reference that violates the setting); pairwise InfoNCE on the random pool.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Diversity-selected pools should beat random ones by about one point, and synthetic pools should match random ones under domain shift. It may fail if the selection criterion favours outliers that carry little shared signal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pool construction at scale: curated, random, synthetic and mixed public sets over many shifts
PROPOSAL: Forty clients with mixed architectures and tasks align on public pools of 200000 samples built five ways: random web images, diversity-selected images, diffusion-generated images, blends, and class-balanced selections. A joint contrastive loss runs 80 rounds with 6 seeds. We compare local accuracy per pool across 6 domain shifts between local data and pool, regenerating the synthetic pools for every shift.
CONTROLS: Local-only training; a pool of pure noise images; a pool drawn from the clients' own training data (an upper reference that violates the setting); pairwise InfoNCE on the random pool for each shift.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Diversity-selected pools should beat random ones by about one point, and synthetic pools should match random ones under shift. It may fail if the selection criterion favours outliers that carry little shared signal.
